text: Hi, everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How are we feeling?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're in the home stretch.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: My name is Sarah, and I am a context engineer at PostHog, and I get the delight of working on our beloved wizard every single day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, what's the wizard?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The wizard sets up PostHog for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's an agentic CLI tool that reads your code base, it installs the right SDK for your project, it instruments your events, and it sets up dashboards for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It takes what used to take about an hour or two of setup, and it runs that in about five to six minutes, and it's free inference on us so that you have a great time onboarding to PostHog.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Sounds kind of sick.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: People love it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But a few months ago, we dared to dream, what if this became the recommended or default way to install PostHog on your project?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: My security alarm bell started going off.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I started questioning how secure is this thing because it sounds kind of malware-shaped.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in that questioning, I learned a lot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So today is all about the lessons I learned, the stuff that kept me up at night while I was building this thing, and the thing that I ended up building because of it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So before I dive into all of the boring security stuff, AKA your 2PM catnap, I want to show you the wizard actually running.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you look up on the screen, it is running for you on a loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is the same exact experience that anyone who runs npx at posthog wizard gets on their terminal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like I said, it's an agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It figures out what SDK is right for your project.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It installs it for you, instruments your events, builds dashboards.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I like to call it a little mini implementation engineer in your terminal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And sometimes I show people this and they ask me, why an agent?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Why don't you give users a good prompt?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Why don't you give them a skill that they can invoke in their own tool?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And while we do provide those things, the answer is because this developer experience and the capability of the wizard is the whole point.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's the whole product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because we built a CLI tool that can fully take part in an agent loop, and experiencing that for the first time is really powerful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But you can't ship something like the wizard without shipping the stuff that makes the wizard kind of suspect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's take it apart.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let's look at the anatomy of the wizard because usually threat models fall right out of the anatomy of the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the wizard is a similar shape to what I'm sure a lot of you are building if you're building agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's got models that we've picked for specific tasks, it's got prompts that steer it, and it's got a set of tools that we've handed it to get the job done.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But it also has some pieces that are really specific to us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has a context engine fully built in-house by my team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's what allows the agent to do such a good job and give us similar results on every run.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I like to call it the wizard's brain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Sometimes we call it markdown in a trench coat.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But it's our in-house context engine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's also a terminal UI that we built ourselves using Ink.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And now there's a security scanner called the Warlock, which is what I built when I started snooping around and uncovering the horrors of shipping an agent to production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, if you take the anatomy of any agent that can run commands, it's basically what I like to call the Malware Starter Pack, because it's almost exactly what you would hand a piece of malware if you were feeling generous or chaotic evil.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Luckily, this is the worst case scenario or the nightmare fuel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's not a confession for me.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a warning for all of you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because if you want to ship an agent with hands, an agent that can run commands, you need to make sure that you do not build this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the v0 of the wizard was born because Josh Snyder, if you know him on our growth team, was watching Cursor hallucinate post-hog setups in quite possibly the worst ways.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And he thought, what if we built an agent that could do a better job?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So my team started building on top of it as we validated that it did a much better job than cursor hallucinating.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we thought, what if it could onboard anyone to PostHog?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It doesn't matter what their framework is, what their stack is, instrument all their events without them having to touch a thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we dared to dream, what if it was the default way to install PostHog?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We were dreaming of thousands of developers running this a week, and yesterday we just hit 8,000 people running this a week.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So our dream came true, but back in those days when we were dreaming, we had to take our security posture under a microscope and look at what was going on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I took the ownership of that, and I sat down and evaluated where we stood.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And early on, I'm talking like a year to nine months ago, we had what I call layer zero because it quite literally is not security.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It is just prompts that suggest what the agent should do and steer it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And prompts are not security.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I was concerned there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Layer 1, it was an allow list, and when I started digging into this allow list, I started to feel a little bit better because it was pretty tightly bounded, but I still had a lot of concerns.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I started panicking because of that context engine that I told you about.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We are feeding a lot of context into the agent at runtime, so I built this really hacky regex scanner to look for
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Threat-shaped things going into the wizard and threat-shaped things coming out of the wizard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I will admit that it was extremely hacky.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But I'm telling all of you this very candidly because we are all building things that feel extremely experimental and we are all building things super fast.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I know not all of us have security in our wheelhouse and some of us are just learning it on the fly like I was.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But it's something we need to be thinking about when we are building things that have this shape.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that was our security posture.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But I asked the question, are we cooked?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Good news, we were less cooked than I thought.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because when I mentioned earlier that allow list, it was pretty tightly bound.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We had bash as deny by default.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It could only install trusted packages that were vetted by us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It could build, it could type check, it could lint, and pretty much nothing else.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It couldn't run random shell commands, and it didn't have access to environment variables.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent couldn't read your .env file because we blocked it outright and we were rooting secrets through a vault.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I took a breath of relief and realized we were in a better place than I thought.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But I wanted to know where the cracks were because with security there's always cracks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I did the thing that we should all be doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I tapped our security team and I said, hey, can you audit this thing for me and find those cracks for me?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they found some things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They found some gaps.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the interesting part wasn't the specific gaps or bugs they found themselves, but it was the shape of them, because almost none of them were obviously evil.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They were all two very innocent, well-intentioned things that were shaking hands and opening a hole.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the lesson I learned was that attacks compose, code review doesn't, because us developers all look at diffs one at a time, but attackers look at the whole system and they look for those two things that shake hands and open a door.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But there was one more thing that was keeping me up at night.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And going back to that context engine, I realized the scariest part of the agent we had built wasn't really a command in our case.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was the helpful looking stuff that we were feeding its brain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Oh, I think I went the wrong way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The context mill.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is our context engine, a.k.a.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: the wizard's brain, and it's how the wizard knows anything at all and why the wizard actually does a good job.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It pulls from our docs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has handwritten prompts that are gotchus and lessons that we learned along the way and real working end-to-end example apps that help the agent pattern match so that it can install PostHog in a really great way for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It packages all of that into skill bundles that get shipped to the wizard over our MCP server and loaded straight into the agent's context at runtime.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So sit with that for a second.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a machine whose whole job is to take content and inject it into an agent that can run commands.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, if you were an attacker, you might say, well, what if I just poison the content?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Not the user's code base, not the agent itself, but the actual content.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Say someone opens a pull request on one of our open source repos, because at PostHog we build everything in the open, and they inject something in a markdown file or a seemingly harmless code comment, and we have some sort of like LLM-powered code review going through that, and it says, looks good to me, and ignores it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We may have just shipped a prompt injection payload signed by us into an agent that is running on thousands of developers' machines in a sandbox, but still.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that was the threat that reshaped how I think about security and the wizard, because the dangerous input for us really could come from our own supply chain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what I ended up doing is I started scanning content at both ends of this pipe.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, when a skill gets built and released, and again, when the wizard actually uses it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: My methodology is catch it at the source, assume the source failed, and catch it again at the point of use.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So now I get to introduce the Warlock to you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Building the Warlock was not necessarily damage control.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like I said, we had defense in other ways.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But I built the Warlock because I didn't like telling people, well, this thing is pretty locked down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That doesn't scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's not something you want to ship to production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's not something that you want thousands of developers running every single day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because when you ship something to that scale, you have way more surface, way more users, way more content flowing in as you expand the capability of the wizard, and where probably fine just stops being good enough.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I pulled that hacky little regex scanner that I threw in there, pulled it out of the wizard, and I made a standalone thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I called it the Warlock because everything wizard shape needs a bodyguard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it does exactly one job.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You hand it a string.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It hands you back a list of findings.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Each of those findings has a category, a severity, and a recommended action, and then it stops.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want you to focus on recommended here because the Warlock detects it does not act.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It'll tell you, hey, this looks like exfiltration.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's critical.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I would block it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But what you actually do with that finding is completely up to you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because detecting a problem is one job, and deciding what to do about that problem is a totally different job.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the only thing that keeps all of this understandable is keeping those two things separate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So underneath the hood of the Warlock, instead of my hand-rolled regexes, the rules run on Yara, which is the pattern that Engine malware researchers have been using for, like, 15-plus years.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's fully deterministic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's the same input, same output every single time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's boring on purpose, and in security, boring is a feature.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what does the Warlock actually catch in the wild today?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A bunch of different stuff, but two of these are an absolute nuisance to my soul.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first thing is actually not a rule-shaped thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was something that the Warlock flagged that was actually a sub-agent behavior that exposed a vulnerability to us based off of what sub-agents were doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So basically, we were spinning up agents to do large tasks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They were spawning subagents, and those subagents were trying to get around the guardrails that we had implemented in the wizard, and they were trying to invent secrets.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They were trying to pull secrets from quite literally anywhere in the code base, and we shut it down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We said, no more subagents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And because of the Warlock, we caught that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'll empathize with the robot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The robot had a task to do and it was trying to optimize and please us, but we can't have that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And something else at PostHog that really matters to us is PII.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents genuinely do not care about exposing data unless you make explicit rules.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Left alone, we watched it dump emails, phone numbers straight into events and to an agent that looks like a totally normal thing to capture.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And luckily for prompt injection specifically, I'm going to knock on wood here, we have basically never caught an actual malicious prompt injection in the wild, but we do catch a ton of false positives, things like our demo login screens, copy on our example apps, things in our docs, and it's actually made me rethink how I build applications and how I write docs because I don't want to ship anything that looks threat shaped.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the false positives are honestly the perfect setup for the messiest, most interesting part of this whole thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is the part that I wrestled with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I spent this whole talk preaching deterministic to all of you, and then I went and I added an LLM layer to help sort my false positives and silence some of the noise, and I call it triage.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When I was building this triage layer, I had to make a choice.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Should the layer be a bouncer or should the layer be an advisor?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the easiest choice probably could have been make the LLM the bouncer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Show it the command, ask it, is this an attack, block, allow, and just do whatever it says.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And while that's tempting because it seems easier, I can't bet my security model on a coin flip because my model's having a bad day or something happened and it's acting different today than it did yesterday.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So instead of the bouncer, I crafted the model to be the advisor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this was the clean line that I found in a line that I'm still exploring, but I want to leave all of you with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For us, detection and enforcement stay deterministic and mechanical.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If a rule matches, the gate locks, the session ends, and there is no model anywhere on that path.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The block happens before we even ask the LLM's opinion.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The LLM only gets to weigh in afterwards if we have not blocked something.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's designed to remove noise.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It is not designed to let things through.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if it fails closed, so if the model is having a bad day, all wizard runs are killed, sorry, but we're just protecting you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Enforcement is the part that you bet the house on, so it has to be deterministic, but judgment is the part that adds nuance, so that's really the only place that you can put anything probabilistic in there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So how do we ship real rules for agents?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is the anatomy of one of our Warlock rules.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And every Warlock rule has four parts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Part one is the metadata.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's plain English description, severity, category, action, direction.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Is this flowing into the agent?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Is this something the agent is writing?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then we have the strings.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So these are the actual patterns that you're looking for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And part three is the condition.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is where the rule is actually allowed to fire.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'll walk through this example for you, and we can pretend like we're writing it in our head.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Prompt injection being like the classic ignore all previous instructions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your first instinct here is probably to block the word ignore, but agents read code all day and ignore can show up in code comments or examples all the time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you don't want to match the verb alone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You match the verb plus an instruction flavored noun.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the condition, you say fire if any of those patterns hit.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in the metadata, you determine is this critical, what the category is, what the action is, in this case block, and the direction, in this case being input flowing into the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But to write good rules that reduce noise, you have to ship tests with them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you have to write tests that say these are patterns that match, these are ones that should not.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that negative test is the first line of defense against false positives.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But you also want to make sure when you're deciding the severity of that rule that you track real-world impact, not how scary it looks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: RM-RF is scary, but it's also how we all delete node modules like 40 times a day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You decide the real-world impact
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: for the agent that you're building because a security tool that crashes every time it tries to clean a build folder is a tool that gets turned off and one that catches absolutely nothing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I'm proud to say this is our security posture now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I can finally come up here and say we have true defense in depth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All my learnings have
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Assembled into this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's still layered, but every layer is doing a job that it's good at now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We still have prompts, but we only use them for steering.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Everything runs in a sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We deny by default.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a vault so secrets never hit the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have the warlock to scan content coming in and to scan output being written by the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also have triage to reduce the noise, and we have telemetry embedded in the entire process so that we see everything.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: None of these layers stands on its own.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Not a single thing here is going to save you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But it's just boring, honest layers, each of them doing one job that it's good at.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if you're building an agent with hands, this is the whole talk in three lines.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, if it isn't enforced deterministically, it is not enforced.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Prompts are not security rules.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Don't act like they are.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two, the dangerous input isn't just what your user types.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It isn't just the commands that you allow it to run.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's everything flowing into the model, including the content that you write yourself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So scan your own supply chain at the source and when the agent invokes it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Three, attacks compose, code review doesn't.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Most of our gaps during our audit were two innocent things, shaking hands and opening a door.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The Wizard, the Warlock, and the context mill are all open source.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So come find me downstairs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm in the expo hall at our booth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'll show you around, show you what we built.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I want to hear how you guys are securing your agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you.
